passages.title: From running machine to safety bicycle
passages.text:
A  Today the bicycle looks like a simple machine, but it took about seventy years to reach the shape that most people ride now. Each step in its story solved one problem and often created another.

B  The first step came in 1817. On 12 June that year, Karl Drais rode his "running machine" from the German city of Mannheim. It had two wheels but no pedals: the rider sat on it and pushed it along the ground with his feet while steering. On this first reported ride, Drais covered about 13 kilometres in less than an hour. Why did he build it? His biographer has suggested, from indirect evidence, that Drais was looking for an alternative to the horse after a failed harvest in 1816 had caused many horses to die of hunger.

C  In the early 1860s, two Frenchmen, Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement, took the design in a new direction. They fixed a crank with pedals to a larger front wheel, so riders could finally keep their feet off the ground. These machines became known as "boneshakers", a name that says a lot about how they felt on rough roads.

D  Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, a bigger wheel carried the rider further with each turn of the pedals, and so allowed higher speeds. In the 1870s this idea produced the high-wheeler, often called the penny-farthing, with a very large front wheel. It was fast, but the rider sat high above the ground, and falls were dangerous: two broken wrists were a common result when riders put out their hands to stop a fall.

E  The solution was the "safety bicycle". In 1885, John Kemp Starley produced the first successful one, the Rover. Its two wheels were about the same size, and a chain carried power from the pedals to the rear wheel, so the wheel no longer had to be huge to go fast. Three years later, in 1888, the Scotsman John Boyd Dunlop introduced the first practical air-filled, or pneumatic, tyre, which made riding far more comfortable. With these two changes, the bicycle had taken the basic form that we still recognise.

passages.title: Why cities are warmer
passages.text:
A  On a calm summer evening, a city can feel noticeably warmer than the countryside around it. Scientists call this an "urban heat island": an urban area that is significantly warmer than the rural areas that surround it because of human activities.

B  The difference is usually larger at night than during the day. It is also most apparent when winds are weak.

C  One cause is the surfaces that cities are built from. Dark surfaces, such as asphalt roads, absorb much more of the sun's energy than fields and forests do. City materials also store a great deal of heat, and after sunset these still-warm surfaces keep the air above them warm. A second cause is the lack of plants. Plants release water into the air, and this process, called evapotranspiration, cools their surroundings. Where roads and buildings replace vegetation, much of this natural cooling disappears.

D  The way buildings are arranged matters too. Tall buildings standing close together create narrow "urban canyons" that can trap heat. People and their machines add heat as well: cars, factories and air-conditioning systems all produce waste heat. Air conditioning, in particular, can lead to higher temperatures at night.

E  Cities can reduce the effect. Planting trees brings back shade and some of the natural cooling that plants provide. Green roofs, which are covered with plants, work in a similar way. Another approach is to use lighter-coloured surfaces, which reflect more sunlight instead of absorbing it. None of these ideas is likely to remove a heat island completely, but together they can make city streets more comfortable in hot weather.

passages.title: The long road of paper
passages.text:
A  Few inventions are as easy to overlook as paper. It wraps our food, fills our notebooks and carries our money, yet for most of human history it did not exist. Its journey from China to Europe lasted many centuries, and the story people usually tell about it is not quite the one the evidence supports.

B  Tradition gives the credit to Cai Lun, an imperial official of the Han dynasty, and dates his invention to 105 CE. He is said to have made paper from mulberry and other plant fibres, together with fishing nets, old rags and waste hemp. Archaeology, however, complicates this picture. The oldest surviving fragment of paper, found at Fangmatan in Gansu province, has been dated to between 179 and 141 BCE, well over two centuries before Cai Lun. It seems, then, that he improved and standardised a craft that already existed rather than creating it from nothing.

C  From China, the craft travelled west. Paper was in use in Central Asia by the 8th century, and Samarkand in particular became known for it: one historical account describes the city as famous for making paper and says its paper was exported to many other cities. A popular story links the arrival of papermaking in Samarkand to Chinese prisoners captured at the Battle of Talas in 751, who supposedly taught the craft to their captors. Historians are sceptical; one has called the connection unlikely to be factual. The story is memorable, but memorability is not evidence.

D  Further west, paper took hold in Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid caliphate. During the 8th century it began to replace parchment, which is made from animal skin, as the main writing material for government business there, and scholars have identified paper mills worked by people or animals in the city in the 790s. By the end of the 9th century, paper had become more popular than papyrus across the Muslim world.

E  Europe came to paper late, and through Spain, where much of the land was then under Muslim rule. The oldest known paper document in Europe, the Mozarab Missal of Silos, dates from the 11th century, and the first recorded paper mill on the Iberian Peninsula was at Xàtiva in 1056.

F  Looking back, the history of paper seems less the tale of one inventor than of a craft passed from place to place and improved along the way. That may be less romantic than a single moment of genius, but it is probably closer to the way most technologies develop.

passages.title: Tardigrades: survivors, not superheroes
passages.text:
A  If you collect some damp moss and look at it under a microscope, you may find a tardigrade. These tiny animals, also known as water bears or moss piglets, are usually about 0.5 millimetres long when fully grown, although the largest species can reach 1.3 millimetres. They have short, plump bodies and four pairs of legs, each ending in claws.

B  The German zoologist Johann August Ephraim Goeze first described them in 1773, calling them "little water bears". In 1776, the Italian biologist Lazzaro Spallanzani gave the group its scientific name, Tardigrada, which means "slow walkers".

C  Tardigrades live in a remarkable range of places, from mountaintops and tropical rainforests to the deep sea and the Antarctic. What has made them famous, however, is not where they live but what they can survive.

D  When their surroundings dry out, tardigrades can enter a state known as cryptobiosis. They draw in their legs and form a dried-out body called a "tun", in which no metabolic activity takes place. In this condition they can wait until water returns and then become active again.

E  In 2007, researchers put this ability to an extreme test. Samples of tardigrades and their eggs were taken into orbit on the FOTON-M3 mission and exposed to the vacuum of space. The vacuum alone had no significant effect on them. When it was combined with ultraviolet radiation, however, many of the tuns were killed.

F  It is tempting to call tardigrades indestructible, but that would be misleading. Scientists do not regard them as true extremophiles, that is, organisms adapted to exploit extreme conditions. Tardigrades are not adapted to make use of many of the harsh conditions they have been tested in; they can only endure them.

passages.title: Qanats: rivers beneath the desert
passages.text:
A  In hot, dry regions, the difficulty with water is not only finding it but moving it. Water carried across open country in surface channels is exposed to sun and wind, and much of it can evaporate before it reaches the fields. Roughly three thousand years ago, the ancient Iranians developed an ingenious answer: the qanat, an underground channel that carries water from an aquifer or a well to the surface.

B  The principle is simple, even if the construction is not. Water drains along the channel by gravity, typically from an aquifer in higher ground towards a destination that lies lower than the source, so no pumps are required. Along the route, vertical shafts are dug down to the tunnel at intervals. They support the construction and maintenance of the underground channel, and they also allow air to circulate. Most qanats in Iran are less than five kilometres long, but some near the city of Kerman run for roughly seventy kilometres.

C  Keeping the water underground brings a decisive advantage. Shielded from the heat of the surface, a qanat can move water over long distances in a hot, dry climate without much of it being lost to evaporation. And because it is powered only by gravity, it has low running costs compared with systems that need fuel or electricity.

D  The technique travelled widely, and under several names. Similar systems are called kārēz in Afghanistan and Pakistan and foggāra in Algeria, and in China they form part of the Turpan water system in Xinjiang. In Europe, qanat-style channels were introduced under the Roman Empire, and they were later built on a larger scale in Muslim-ruled Spain.

E  None of this means that qanats look after themselves. Their channels must be inspected regularly for erosion and cave-ins, cleaned of sand and mud, and repaired. In many regions, a more serious threat has come from outside: wells fitted with pumps, together with heavy pumping of groundwater, have lowered water tables, and many qanats have dried up and been abandoned as a result.

F  Their value has not been forgotten. In 2016, eleven qanats were inscribed together on UNESCO's World Heritage List as "The Persian Qanat". To the writer, they carry a lesson that goes beyond engineering: a durable solution need not be a high-tech one, and some of the oldest answers to scarcity may still deserve a place in modern planning.

passages.title: The shape of forgetting
passages.text:
A  In 1885, the German psychologist Hermann Ebbinghaus published a book on memory, later translated into English as Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology. In it he did something that seems obvious now but was new at the time: he treated memory as something that could be measured. He is widely regarded as the pioneer of the experimental study of memory.

B  His method demanded patience. From 1880 to 1885 he acted as the only subject of his own study, memorising lists of nonsense syllables: meaningless combinations of a consonant, a vowel and another consonant, such as WID or ZOF. He chose them deliberately. Since learning is affected by prior knowledge, he needed material that could be memorised but that carried no existing associations, so that his results would reflect memory itself rather than what he already knew.

C  By testing himself after different delays, Ebbinghaus traced what is now called the forgetting curve. It falls steeply at first and then levels off: much of what is learned is lost soon afterwards, while what survives that early loss fades more slowly. He is also credited with the first description of the learning curve and with discovering the spacing effect, the finding that learning is more effective when study sessions are spaced out than when they are crowded together.

D  The limits of his work are plain. A study with a single participant, using material without meaning, cannot simply be generalised to everyone or to everything people learn. Yet its central result has proved durable. In 2015, an attempt to replicate the forgetting curve, again with one subject, produced results similar to Ebbinghaus's original data.

E  For students, the spacing effect may be the most useful part of this legacy. Studying the same material in several shorter sessions spread over time is more effective than cramming it into a single long one. Spaced repetition, which shows new and difficult material more often and familiar material less often, is built on this effect, and it is used in a number of flashcard programs.

F  What impresses the writer most, however, is not the result but the attitude behind it. Faced with something as elusive as memory, Ebbinghaus did not wait for a perfect method. He chose a simple one and applied it patiently over several years. That habit of mind may be as valuable to a student today as any memory technique.

passages.title: A safe place for the world’s seeds
passages.text:
A  Farmers around the world grow thousands of different kinds of wheat, rice, beans and other crops. Many of these kinds are grown in only a few places, and a flood, a fire or a war could destroy them for ever. For this reason, seed banks keep samples of seeds, so that a lost crop can be grown again.

B  A seed bank can be damaged too, so many seed banks send a second copy of their seeds to a store on the Arctic island of Spitsbergen. The Svalbard Global Seed Vault officially opened there on 26 February 2008. It is not a building on the surface: the seeds lie 130 metres inside a sandstone mountain.

C  The store is designed to stay cold and dry. Its storage rooms are kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius. If the electricity supply ever fails, the frozen ground around the rooms, called permafrost, will help to keep the seeds at a low temperature. The site is also high enough to stay dry even if the ice caps melt. Even so, the design has been tested: in October 2016, an unusually large amount of water came into the entrance tunnel. It reached 15 metres into the tunnel before it froze.

D  The vault has room for 4.5 million seed samples, and each bag holds about 500 seeds on average. By June 2025 it held more than 1.3 million samples. The seeds still belong to the seed bank that sent them. Only that bank has the right to take its own samples out, and no one has access to another bank’s seeds.

E  The first withdrawal came in 2015. A research centre called ICARDA could no longer keep up its seed bank at Tel Hadya in Syria, so it took back some of the copies it had stored in the vault, in order to grow them again. The seeds were planted in fields in Lebanon and Morocco, where they were multiplied. In this way, the copies in the Arctic did exactly the job they had been sent there to do.

passages.title: The observatory of Ulugh Beg
passages.text:
A  In the 1420s, the Timurid astronomer Ulugh Beg built an observatory in Samarkand, a city in what is now Uzbekistan. The building was completed around 1428. An observatory is a place for studying the sky, and this one was built on a very large scale.

B  The main building was round, like a short and very wide tower. It had a diameter of 46 metres and was between 30 and 33 metres high. Inside, it was made up of three storeys, so the building itself was as tall as a modern block of flats of about ten floors.

C  At its heart stood the observatory’s main instrument, a huge curved scale made with marble and often called the Fakhri sextant. Its radius was about 40 metres. Size mattered here: a bigger curve has room for finer marks, so an astronomer using it could read the position of a star more exactly than with a small one.

D  What did all this work produce? Ulugh Beg’s star catalogue, the Zij-i Sultani, listed around 1,000 stars. A catalogue of this kind gives the position of each star in the sky, so that other astronomers can find the same star again.He also determined the length of the year as 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes and 15 seconds.

E  The observatory did not last long. It was destroyed in 1449, around the time of Ulugh Beg’s assassination by his own son, Abd al-Latif. More than 450 years then passed before anyone uncovered what was left of it.

F  In 1908, the Russian archaeologist Vassily Vyatkin uncovered the remains of the observatory. Today, the foundations and the part of the marble instrument that lies below the ground are all that can be seen. Even so, the curve of that instrument still shows how large the original must have been.

passages.title: How honeybees share directions
passages.text:
A  When a honeybee finds a good source of food, it can tell other bees in its colony where to go. It does this with a set of movements known as the waggle dance. The Austrian scientist and Nobel Prize winner Karl von Frisch was one of the first people to work out what the dance means. The dance does two jobs: it points the way, and it tells the other bees how far to fly.

B  Honeybees that nest in hollow spaces dance in the dark, on the upright surface of the honeycomb. They cannot see the Sun there, so they use gravity instead. A waggle run that goes straight up the comb means “fly directly towards the Sun”. A run at an angle to the right or left of straight up means “fly at the same angle to the right or left of the Sun”.

C  The dance also gives distance, which is coded in how long each waggle run lasts. When the food is very close, up to about ten metres from the hive, bees perform a simpler round dance instead. The full waggle dance is used for food more than about 40 metres away, and a mixture of the two is seen in between.

D  A dancing bee may repeat its movements anywhere from once to more than a hundred times. Other bees follow the dancer closely, but they do not rely on its movements alone. A follower may also use the scent of the flowers that the dancer carries, and it may then find either the same flowers or different ones with a similar smell.

E  Following a dance does not always lead straight to food. Some bees watch more than 50 waggle runs and still fail to find the source, while others set off successfully after watching only five.

F  The dance is also not the only way in which bees decide where to go. In one experiment, 93 per cent of foragers went back to areas they already knew, and the use of the information in dances has been put as low as ten per cent of the time. The dance, then, is one source of information among several.

passages.title: Penicillin: from a spoiled dish to a medicine
passages.text:
A  At the end of July 1928, Alexander Fleming, a bacteriologist at St Mary’s Hospital in London, left his laboratory for a holiday. Before he went, he set up a number of culture plates, the shallow dishes in which bacteria are grown. He returned to the laboratory on 3 September. What he found in one of the dishes is now a famous story.

B  Among the dishes was one whose lid had been left open, and its culture had been spoiled by a blue-green mould. Fleming noticed something unexpected: the bacteria around the mould had not grown. He went on to show that the mould could kill a number of bacteria, among them Staphylococcus.

C  Fleming named the substance “penicillin” on 7 March 1929, and on 10 May that year he reported his findings to the British Journal of Experimental Pathology. However, Fleming was a bacteriologist, not a chemist, and two younger colleagues could not isolate penicillin from the mould, so the chemical work stalled.

D  The next step was taken ten years later, in 1939, at the Sir William Dunn School of Pathology at the University of Oxford. There, a team that included Howard Florey and Ernst Chain developed a method of growing the mould and of extracting, purifying and storing penicillin from it.

E  In February 1941, penicillin was used to treat an infection in a police officer. Within a day of receiving it, he started to recover, but the researchers did not have enough penicillin to help him to a full recovery. The next challenge was clear: to make far more of the drug.

F  The answer came from the United States. At a research laboratory there, scientists grew the mould in large vats instead of shallow dishes, and in 1943 the best sample of the mould was found on a cantaloupe melon sold at a fruit market in Peoria. In 1945, Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

passages.title: How silk is made
passages.text:
A  Silk comes from the cocoons of the silkworm, the young of the silkmoth. Farming silkworms for their silk is called sericulture. Turning the cocoons into something that can be woven takes several steps, and each step has to happen at the right time and in the right order. This passage follows the steps in the order in which they happen.

B  The process begins with eggs. A female silkmoth lays between 300 and 500 of them. When the young worms hatch, they are fed with mulberry leaves. The worms eat and grow, and as they grow they moult, which means that they lose their old skin.

C  After the fourth moult, each worm is ready to spin. It makes its cocoon from one continuous filament, about one mile, or 1.6 kilometres, long, and the work takes it about two or three days. The filament is made of a material called fibroin, and a sticky substance called sericin holds it together. Inside the finished cocoon, the worm becomes a pupa, the stage between worm and moth.

D  Next, the cocoons are heated in water. The heat softens the sericin and removes it, so that the filament comes free and is ready to be unwound. The heat also kills the pupa, the insect that is growing inside the cocoon.

E  The free filament is then unwound from the cocoon. This step is called reeling. Single filaments are combined to form a thread, and one thread can contain up to 48 of them. The thread can then be dyed and woven into cloth.

F  A great many cocoons are needed for even a small amount of cloth. About 2,500 silkworms are required to produce one pound, or roughly 450 grams, of raw silk. A single kilogram of raw silk therefore needs the work of more than 5,000 silkworms.

passages.title: From cacao pod to chocolate
passages.text:
A  Chocolate begins as the seeds of the cacao tree. These seeds, usually called beans, grow inside pods on the tree. Between the farm and the shop, the beans pass through a long series of steps, and each one changes them a little more. This passage follows them in order.

B  First, the pods are harvested. Workers cut them from the tree with a machete, or knock them down with a stick. The pods are opened, and the beans are taken out together with the pulp around them.

C  The beans are not used at once. They are left to ferment, as micro-organisms that are naturally present in the environment start to work on them. Fermentation takes up to seven days, and it produces the substances that will later give chocolate its flavour. Then comes drying: where the weather allows it, the beans are spread out in the sun for five to seven days.

D  At the factory, the beans are cleaned to remove twigs, stones and other waste. They are roasted and graded. Next, the shell of each bean is removed to leave the nib, the inside of the bean. The nibs are ground, and the result is called chocolate liquor.

E  Chocolate liquor can be made into cocoa powder and cocoa butter. To make a bar of chocolate, however, a mixing machine adds milk, sugar and other ingredients to the liquor. The rest of this passage follows the way to a bar.

F  The mixture then goes through conching. This step makes the cocoa and sugar particles smaller than the tongue can detect, and how long it lasts decides how smooth the finished chocolate is. The last step is tempering, in which a small amount of the cocoa butter is made to form crystals. It is the last of the many steps between the farm and the shop.

passages.title: How black tea is made
passages.text:
A  Green tea and black tea look and taste very different, yet both are made from the leaves of the same plant, Camellia sinensis. The types of tea are told apart by the processing they go through after the leaves are picked, and above all by how far the leaves are allowed to oxidise. This passage follows the steps for black tea and notes where green tea is made differently.

B  The first step is plucking. A bud and the two young leaves below it are picked from the bush. These soft young leaves are what all the later steps work on.

C  The fresh leaves are then withered. In a withering room, they are spread out along troughs for eight to fourteen hours, usually overnight. Withering removes excess water from the leaves and lets a very slight amount of oxidation take place.

D  Next comes a step called disruption: the leaves are bruised or torn, so that oxidation starts sooner and goes faster.Often this is done by rolling the leaves, which also makes some of the sap, essential oils and juices inside them ooze out onto the surface.

E  Oxidation can now take place. It is a chemical change caused by contact with the oxygen in the air; a cut apple that turns brown is a familiar example of it. Enzymes in the leaf break down its chlorophyll, and its tannins are released or changed. For black tea, the leaves are allowed to oxidise completely. Green tea, by contrast, has the least oxidation of all.

F  To make green tea, producers stop oxidation early by a step called fixation, or “kill-green”: the leaves are heated moderately, and the heat switches off the enzymes that cause oxidation. Last of all, black tea and green tea alike are dried, which finishes the tea for sale.

passages.title: From milk to cheese
passages.text:
A  Cheese is made from milk, but the change from one to the other takes several careful steps. This passage follows them for a hard cheese, Cheddar, although many of the same ideas apply to other kinds of cheese. Milk is mostly water, and much of the work of making cheese is a way of removing that water while keeping the solid parts of the milk. The steps below are given in the order in which they happen.

B  The process starts in a large container called a cheese vat. The milk, which may first be pasteurised, is brought to a temperature at which bacteria grow well. The bacteria ferment lactose, the natural sugar in milk, and turn it into lactic acid, so the milk slowly becomes more acidic.

C  Next, rennet is added. It causes casein, a protein in milk, to come out of the liquid, and the milk sets into a soft mass called the curd. This is the moment when the liquid milk first becomes something solid. The liquid that is left behind is called whey.

D  For Cheddar, the curd is then cut into small cubes. Cutting lets the whey come out of the curd, and the whey is drained away, leaving the curd firmer and drier than before.

E  Salt is then mixed into the curd, and the salt stops the acid from developing any further; without it, the curd would keep on becoming more acidic. The salted curd is put into cheese moulds lined with cheesecloth and pressed overnight, which gives the cheese its shape.

F  Last comes ripening. The cheese is stored so that it can age, and the time this takes depends on the kind of cheese. A hard cheese may ripen for months or even years, while cheeses ripened by mould are ready far sooner, often within weeks.

passages.title: The cable car to Sarn
passages.text:
A  The village of Sarn sits on a high shelf of rock above the town of Lowmere. For a long time the only way up was a narrow road with twenty-two bends. In winter the road was often closed by snow, and the village could be cut off for days.

B  Ten years ago the two councils agreed to build a cable car. It has twelve small cabins, and each one holds eight people. The ride from the bottom station to the top takes six minutes, and the cabins run every quarter of an hour from six in the morning until midnight.

C  The cable car has changed daily life in Sarn. Children now go down to the secondary school in Lowmere and come home for lunch, and older people can reach the doctor in town without asking a neighbour for a lift. A small shop has also opened next to the top station.

D  Not everyone was happy at first. Some villagers were afraid that crowds of visitors would spoil the quiet streets. To prevent this, tickets for visitors cost three times as much as tickets for people who live in Sarn.

E  Once a year, in early spring, the cable car stops for two weeks so that engineers can check every cable and wheel. During those weeks a minibus takes people up and down the old road, and the village shop stays open for longer hours.
passages.topic: an invented hill village and its cable car
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: The walking bus of Fennick Primary
passages.text:
A  At Fennick Primary School, about sixty children no longer come to school by car. Instead, they walk in a long line with two adults at the front and two at the back. The parents call it the walking bus, because it follows a fixed route and picks children up at stops along the way.

B  The idea came from a group of parents who were worried about the traffic outside the school gate every morning. So many cars stopped there at the same time that it had become dangerous for the children who already walked.

C  There are now three routes, each about one and a half kilometres long. Every child wears a bright yellow coat, which the school bought with money raised at its summer fair. The walking bus runs in all weathers, and in heavy rain the adults carry spare umbrellas.

D  Teachers say that children who walk arrive calmer and more ready to learn than those who come by car. Some of them also say that the walk has helped shy children to make friends with pupils from other classes.

E  The walking bus needs about twenty adult volunteers each week. Most are parents or grandparents, but two are students from the nearby college, who count the hours towards a community award.
passages.topic: an invented school and its walking bus
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: The street fridge in Dunlin Road
passages.text:
A  Outside the corner shop in Dunlin Road stands an ordinary white fridge with a glass door. It is not for sale, and it does not belong to the shop. It is a community fridge, where anyone can leave food they do not need and anyone can take food for free.

B  The fridge was the idea of a nurse called Leyla Osman, who was tired of seeing good food thrown away at the end of the week. She asked the owner of the shop for a place to put it and for electricity, and he agreed at once.

C  There are a few simple rules. Food must be in date and clearly labelled, and nothing that has been cooked at home may be left in the fridge. Raw meat and fish are not allowed either, because they spoil too quickly.

D  Volunteers check the fridge twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. They clean the shelves, remove anything that has passed its date and write in a notebook what has come in and what has gone out.

E  On an average day, more than fifty items pass through the fridge. Bread, fruit and yoghurt disappear fastest. The shop owner says the fridge has brought new customers to his shop too, because people often buy something while they are there.
passages.topic: an invented community fridge
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: Recording the sounds of a town
passages.text:
A  When the last of the weaving sheds in Ambery closed, a retired music teacher, Tomas Reid, realised that the sound of the looms had disappeared from the town without anyone recording it. He decided that the same should not happen to the sounds that were still there, and he set up the Ambery Sound Archive.

B  The archive now holds more than three thousand recordings, made by volunteers with small digital recorders. They include the bells of the old school, the market traders calling out their prices, the hiss of the steam engine at the railway museum and the birds singing at dawn in the park.

C  Recording is harder than it sounds. Volunteers are trained to hold the microphone still, to note the exact time and place of each recording and to wait for a gap in the traffic. A recording without these details is of little use to future listeners, who will want to know what they are hearing.

D  The most popular part of the archive is a map of the town on which visitors can click a street and hear what it sounded like on a particular day. Schools use it to compare the sounds of busy and quiet streets, and some older residents use it simply to remember places they can no longer visit.

E  Not every recording is kept. Each month a small panel listens to the new ones and removes any in which a private conversation can be heard clearly, since the people speaking never agreed to be recorded.
passages.topic: an invented sound archive
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: When the street lights go dim
passages.text:
A  Two years ago the town of Hessle began dimming its street lights between midnight and five in the morning. The lights are not switched off completely; they shine at about a third of their normal strength, which is still enough to see the pavement clearly.

B  The main reason was cost. The electricity bill of the town for street lighting had doubled in five years, and the council had to choose between dimming the lights and closing one of its two libraries. After a public meeting, most residents voted to keep the library.

C  Some people feared that darker streets would mean more crime. The police officers of the town kept careful records during the first year and found no rise in burglaries or car thefts at night. They believe that the people who might commit such crimes were never put off by bright lights in the first place.

D  An unexpected result came from the amateur astronomers of the town. With less light in the sky, they could see far more stars from the edge of town, and their club, which once had a dozen members, now has more than sixty.

E  Not every street has been dimmed. Lights stay at full strength on the two roads with the most traffic and at every pedestrian crossing, because drivers need to see people crossing even late at night.
passages.topic: an invented town that dims its street lights
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: A museum that lends its collection
passages.text:
A  Most museums keep their objects behind glass. The small museum in Carran does the opposite: about a quarter of its collection can be borrowed by schools, care homes and local clubs, in the same way that books are borrowed from a library.

B  The scheme began almost by accident. A storeroom flooded, and while it was being repaired, the staff had nowhere to put several hundred everyday objects, such as old irons, toys and kitchen tools. Rather than pay for storage, they offered to lend them to anyone who would look after them.

C  Each object travels in a padded box with a card that explains what it is, how old it is and how it was used. Borrowers may handle the objects, but they must wear cotton gloves for anything made of metal or paper, which can be damaged by the oils on human skin.

D  Of course, objects are sometimes broken. The museum accepts this as the price of the scheme and only lends things of which it has several copies. Valuable or rare pieces stay in the building, where visitors can see them on guided tours.

E  The loans have changed who comes to the museum. Many children who first held an object at school later ask their parents to bring them to see the rest of the collection, and the number of visitors has grown every year since the scheme began.
passages.topic: an invented museum that lends objects
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: How the Tellow workshop makes soap
passages.text:
A  The Tellow soap workshop is a small family business in an old stable. It makes about two hundred bars of soap a week, all by hand, and sells them at markets and in two shops in the town. Every bar goes through the same steps.

B  First, the oils are weighed and warmed. The workshop uses olive oil and sunflower oil, which are heated gently in a large steel pot until they are just warm to the touch.

C  Next, the oils are mixed with lye, a strong liquid that turns oil into soap. This is the only dangerous step, so it is always done by the oldest son, who wears thick gloves and safety glasses. The mixture is stirred with a wooden paddle until it becomes as thick as custard.

D  At this point, dried herbs or crushed lavender are added for colour and smell. The thick mixture is then poured into long wooden moulds lined with baking paper, and the moulds are covered with an old blanket to keep them warm.

E  After two days, the soap is hard enough to cut. It is sliced into bars with a wire cutter, and the bars are laid on shelves made of pine. There they must rest for six weeks, so that they become milder and last longer.
passages.topic: an invented soap workshop and its steps
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: From old clothes to a rag rug
passages.text:
A  At the Brennan community centre, a group of volunteers makes rugs from clothes that are too worn to give away. A rug takes about three weeks to finish, and each one is sold at the spring fair of the centre. Most of the volunteers learned the craft from their grandmothers, and they now teach it to younger members.

B  The work starts with sorting. Clothes arrive in bags from local families, and the volunteers sort them by colour into large baskets. Buttons and zips are cut off and kept in jars, because they are used again on other projects.

C  Next, the clothes are cut into long strips about two centimetres wide. Cotton is the easiest material to work with; wool is used only for small rugs, because it is heavier.

D  The strips are then pushed one by one through a piece of strong sacking, using a tool called a prodder, which looks like a thick wooden pencil. The volunteers work from the middle of the rug outwards, so that the pattern stays even.

E  Finally, the back of the rug is covered with a layer of felt, which is sewn on by hand. This stops the strips from being pulled out when people walk on the rug.
passages.topic: an invented community centre that makes rag rugs
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: How the Skarra smokehouse smokes its fish
passages.text:
A  On the island of Skarra, one small smokehouse still prepares fish in the old way. It smokes mainly herring and mackerel, which are caught by local boats early in the morning and brought to the smokehouse the same day.

B  The fish are first cleaned and then left in a tub of salty water for about an hour. The salt helps the fish to keep for longer and gives it a stronger taste.

C  After that, the fish are hung in pairs on long wooden rods called speats. They are left near an open window for a few hours, until the skin feels dry and slightly sticky.

D  The rods are then moved into the smoking room, a tall, narrow building with a fire on the floor. The fire is made from oak chips and sawdust, which burn slowly and give plenty of smoke but little flame. The fish hang above it for up to twelve hours.

E  When the fish have turned a deep golden brown, they are taken down, cooled and packed in boxes lined with greaseproof paper. Most are sold in the two shops on the island, but some are sent by post to customers on the mainland.
passages.topic: an invented island smokehouse and its steps
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: How felt rugs are made in the Oren valley
passages.text:
A  In the villages of the Oren valley, felt rugs are still made by groups of neighbours working together, much as they were a century ago. A large rug needs the wool of about fifteen sheep and a full day of hard work from six or seven people.

B  The wool is sheared in late spring, when the animals no longer need their thick winter coats. It is washed in the river, dried in the sun and then beaten with long willow sticks. The beating loosens the fibres and shakes out any remaining dirt and seeds.

C  The loose wool is then laid out on a large reed mat in several thin layers, each one at right angles to the one below. This crossing of the fibres is what gives the finished felt its strength. Hot water mixed with a little whey from the dairy is sprinkled over the layers until they are soaked through.

D  Next, the mat is rolled up tightly around a pole, with the wet wool inside, and tied with rope. A donkey then pulls the roll up and down the village street for several hours. The pressure and the heat of the water make the fibres lock together.

E  When the roll is opened, the wool has shrunk by about a third and become a single sheet of felt. It is rinsed in cold water to remove the whey, stretched to the right shape and left to dry on the grass for two or three days.
passages.topic: an invented valley and how its felt rugs are made
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: Building with mud bricks in Kesh
passages.text:
A  When the village of Kesh decided to build a new classroom, the villagers chose to make the walls from mud bricks, as their grandparents had done. The material was free, the work could be shared, and the thick walls would keep the room cool in summer and warm in winter.

B  The right soil is the first requirement. The builders dug clay-rich earth from a field beside the river and mixed it with sand, because clay alone cracks badly as it dries. Chopped straw was then added to bind the mixture together.

C  The mixture was soaked with water and trodden by foot for most of a day, until it was smooth and could hold its shape. It was then pressed into open wooden frames, each the size of two bricks, set out on flat ground that had been swept clean.

D  The frames were lifted away almost at once, leaving the wet bricks to dry in the open. After three days the bricks were turned on their sides so that they would dry evenly, and after three weeks they were stacked in loose piles, with gaps between them for the wind to pass through.

E  Only bricks that rang with a clear note when tapped with a stone were used for the walls. Bricks that gave a dull sound were broken up, soaked again and remade. Once the walls were built, they were covered with a thin layer of lime plaster to protect them from rain.
passages.topic: an invented village that builds a classroom of mud bricks
passages.author: agent:p12-iere-b

passages.title: How the Linnet bindery repairs an old book
passages.text:
A  The Linnet bindery repairs old books for libraries, schools and private owners. Most of the books that arrive are not rare; they are cookery books, school prizes and diaries that matter more to their owners than to anyone else.

B  Every repair begins with a careful look at the damage. The binder writes down the size of the book, the kind of paper and any loose or missing pages, and photographs each page that will be taken apart, so that it can be put back exactly as it was.

C  If the spine is broken, the old cover is removed and the pages are separated into their sewn groups, called sections. Any torn pages are mended with thin tissue paper and a paste made from wheat starch, which can be removed later if needed. Glue from the hardware shop is never used, because it turns yellow and cannot be undone.

D  The sections are then sewn together again on a wooden frame, using waxed hemp thread. This is the slowest stage: a thick book may take a whole day to sew. Once the sewing is finished, a strip of cloth is glued along the spine to make it strong.

E  Finally, the book is given a cover. Whenever possible, the binder reuses the original one, cleaning it with a soft brush and repairing its corners with leather. A new cover is made only when the old one is too badly damaged to save.
passages.topic: an invented bindery and how it repairs a book
